utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you were in midstream yesterday. The Chamber will endeavour to ensure that doesn't happen again. You may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if the Chamber still has the document that was distributed yesterday. If not, we do have further copies. May it be made available to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While it's coming, Mr. Stevanovic, you might recall that yesterday we were looking at a different document from that which is being distributed. We were looking at a document of the 2nd of June to Stojiljkovic and others which got an incorrectly attached last page but which referred to Ministry of Interior special units arriving at the institution at 5.00 on the 22nd of May. Now, would you please be good enough to look at this document. This is a document, if you'd look at the last page, that comes from the warden, Aleksandar Rakocevic, who is referred to in other documentation, and then we go to the front page and we'll see what it's all about. On the first page it says it goes to the Ministry of Justice in Belgrade. Incidentally, before I forget the point, was the person at your rank in the Ministry of Justice also called Stevanovic at that time but with a different first name?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was one such person in my position, and there were several other assistants to the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this document, we see that it's a report on the NATO Air Force attack. First of all, it deals with the 19th of May, but if the Chamber would like to look at the foot of the first page -- or if Mr. Prendergast would lay the foot of the first page on the ground, we can see that it says this: "The main building was destroyed," et cetera, and then: "We placed the convicts temporarily on the sports ground." If we move on then to the second page please, which again I'm not going to go through. We can see it covers matters on the 21st of May, with bombing until 1030 hours, the death of the deputy warden --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I cannot hear the interpretation very well. Could the volume be turned up. Yes, it's better now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see it goes on in the second page in English, and in thereabouts, I think, in your document to deal with the 21st with the death of the warden and with dozens killed or injured, the arrival of the journalists, the arrival of the investigative judge. And then on page 3 in the English, it says: "Immediately after the journalists left --" and this is, I think, also at page 3 of yours: "-- and headed towards the main road, the attack started, during which the complete infrastructure was destroyed." It says this: "According to our visual estimate, about 500 [sic] convicts were killed, the majority of them buried under the wreckage."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll see you said 500, Mr. Nice. It's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, no. I said 100, sorry. If I said 500, my error.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then it says the parking bay were hit by missiles, and then this: "On the 22nd of May at about 0500 hours, a special MUP unit arrived and entered the closed section of the Institution. Following an order by this special MUP unit, the security service employees were withdrawn to the broader radius around the circular wall. We do not know what they were doing there, but we could hear detonations. The same MUP unit arrived again around 1700 hours, as well as on the 23rd ... at around 0500 hours." It concludes by saying: "On the 24th, at about 0600 hours in the morning another MUP unit arrived with ten buses and three trucks, which evacuated the convicts into an unknown direction, and this finished about 0900." Now, working in reverse order, is the 24th of May's MUP unit the unit you've spoken about, the evacuation unit?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that would follow from this here. It's a bit odd that the warden doesn't know that they were sent to Lipjan but, rather, he says in an unknown direction. I find this a bit odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe he wasn't told. How do you know that he was told?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to what the warden sets out as having happened at 5.00 in the morning. It matches the document provided by the accused with the curious ending to it, and it says that it was followed by the sound of detonations. Do you know anything about this, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know absolutely nothing about this. This is the first time I've heard of anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, not the first time you've heard of it if you'd reviewed the document in the accused's bundle that we looked at yesterday. But maybe - help us - did you not focus your attention on the 5.00 in the morning reference to the arrival of the special forces when you reviewed the documents ahead of coming to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to review all the documents, and I've already answered your question once and I told you that I was unable to look at each and every document in detail. Of course the details of this quotation that you read out are something I remember from the document we saw yesterday. These details relate to the entry of police units at 500 hours and these other two times, but I don't remember that in the document we saw yesterday it was mentioned that detonations were heard. Of course, it doesn't say here what sort of detonations they were or what caused them, but it was not mentioned in the document we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're quite right, and well spotted. Nor does this document suggest in any way that the detonations were bombing. It would have said bombing if so. Is the truth this, Mr. Stevanovic, a truth that you actually know, and as I suggested to you yesterday, there was a plan, cynically, to kill all the Albanian prisoners in that prison and later to blame it on the NATO bombing? Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can provide this Chamber with no explanation of or account of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was it only Albanians who were killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can elaborate on that. It was only Albanians who were killed, and although we don't have time to explore everything with this witness, the Prosecution's case on this would be that there were a limited number of Serb prisoners held in the prison, not -- not necessarily held exclusively -- in exclusively Serb units, but held in units where they were not exposed to risk from KLA or thought to be KLA supporters. I think it was in unit number 6, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The evidence has been -- in your case evidence was adduced on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I'm just explaining what the position would be. But certainly none of them was killed as a result of what happened, and whether they were separated or not I don't know, but they weren't killed, as I understand it, none of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your suggestions should be based on the case that you have presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. And to some extent it's based on -- of course, when I put matters in detail it's based on additional information that's coming my way and that may be the subject of applications either for rebuttal or to reopen the case. And I've made it clear through my questions to this witness that some of the material I'm putting to him is recently obtained, including from the documents but also from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your answers here about Dubrava, you didn't consider, maybe you didn't have a chance to consider, some of the evidence that's available in this case and indeed is part of the case. Were you aware that a Danish forensic military team examined the prison in August of 1999 and took a video of what it found?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll play it to you, or some very limited extract from it for you, and I'm going to ask you if you'd like to comment on the things that we see or, alternatively, to review your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video itself is about an hour and a half long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, we see here, do we not, an aerial view of this very large prison. We see an aerial view of this very large prison, with a perimeter wall, a series of buildings laid out in a, I suppose, broadly square shape, and at one end of it we can see the sports field. There we see, I think, the sports field on the right but it's going out of view. And here we see, I think, some of the blocks for holding prisoners. You yourself had overflown this, hadn't you, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1998, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see clearly the results of one bomb on that building, but we see other buildings which have not got bomb holes through their roofs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. I think that's enough of that. Next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 165, tab 8, the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Nine hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it nine hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't seen this actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't viewed it, but it's been produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, here this is an inside area, and what you're looking for, or what we're looking at is can you see pockmarks on the floor? We'll see more of them in subsequent clips. We see pockmarks on the floor, and you can see pockmarks on the -- you can see pockmarks on the wall. Now, Mr. Stevanovic, in your experience are those consistent with the shrapnel from hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This might be shrapnel from a hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A room with it looks like bedding and similar in it. Pockmarks on the floor, you can see, or shrapnel marks on the floor. Next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see shrapnel marks on the wall and on the ceiling, on the ventilator duct, if that's what it is. Pausing there, please. You see a hole there in a duct of some kind, I think. Mr. Stevanovic, what you've seen so far, is that -- you're a senior policeman with the rank of general at the time or before this time. Is what you've seen consistent with hand grenades and/or gunfire within those rooms?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give you any opinion about that because I have never had occasion to see such traces. Forensic technicians would be in a better position to talk about this. I can see traces that might be fragments from larger bombs, but I do not consider myself an expert on this, and I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just pause that for a minute. If we can just stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see traces that might be fragments from larger bombs. Traces of what? These are enclosed buildings with roofs and ceilings intact, subject to some damage. What do you say is a trace of what might be a fragment from a larger bomb, if you're not an expert?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're referring to. What I can see here are scraps of paper or sheeting or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I was asking you about your previous answer. You said you saw traces of something that might be fragments from larger bombs. I wanted you to tell us what you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't claiming that these were traces of larger bombs. I was trying to explain that I cannot confirm that they were traces of hand grenades, because the kind of traces I saw do not have associations in my mind with any kind of bomb. Obviously these are fragments, but I cannot really say what kind of explosive device they came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two separate issues there. What was being pointed out to you was marks on the wall, but am I right in thinking you're referring to what you see as pieces of material that may have come from an explosive device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain that the traces I saw on the walls and the floor, according to what experience I have, might originate from fragments of different kinds of explosive devices, but I'm unable to associate these with any kind of specific explosive device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was just that you used the expression - at least the way it was translated earlier - was "fragments from larger bombs," but it's not -- you were talking about marks on the wall rather than pieces of material, or were you talking of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was referring to the traces on the wall which were caused by fragments coming from some sort of explosive device. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we restart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, isn't the truth that the witness can't help us very much on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness has tried to help us from a range of material, giving us a concluded version of what happened at Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I mean this question of where the fragments came from. He doesn't have the expertise. He has said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He doesn't have the expertise and he hasn't considered this material, and it may be -- and all the other material of a forensic scientific kind, to which I was going to refer in summary, then it may be his evidence on this topic is necessarily and inevitably quite valueless for there is a great deal of forensic scientific in the materials already produced. Not just this film. There are two written reports which deal with the findings, and I wanted this witness to have a chance to deal with some of the more obvious points from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not embracing your wider proposition. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, you see, is the area where the prisoners, having been released after the first bombing to sleep, were found. We can see an inspection tower in the corner, or a watchtower in the corner, and the wall. Now, help us: If I suggest to you, as I do, that there are no bomb craters found in this area at all and never were found, are you in any position to contradict me?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot contradict you because I have no knowledge of this. I was never in this place. This is the first time I've seen this film, and anything I say would be speculation. I am not a forensic expert. I am not an expert on explosives. Of course I will answer all your questions if I know the answer. In this case I have spoken only of what I know, but I do not know anything about what you are asking me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I may come back to just a couple more pictures from the scientific reports but otherwise I'll leave the question of Dubrava and analysis of the evidence for subsequent argument, but we will return to two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look next at tab 205.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Binder 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a composition of papers produced by the accused, and the part I'm looking at and concerned to look at is the record of on-site investigation. We can just look briefly at that. Do you have the record of on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn to the last page of it, three pages in English and I suspect the same in your Serbian version, we see -- yes. I said it's a composition of papers, but it's on the on-site investigation report and three pages and as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there are several of these. Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not it, Mr. Prendergast. That's Official Note. Third page of on-site investigation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. It's the -- the way I have it in the bundle I have is in three pages. Does Your Honour have one in three pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've got one in three pages with an Official Note as a fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. That's the one, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 3 and the Official Note is page 4 in my version, which is a copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we can -- if you turn to the third page, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to help the witness find his way around, as well as Mr. Nice. In this tab, there are three attachments. Attachment number 3 is the record of on-site investigation, which in the original has two pages. I hope the witness can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then in the same tab we have attachment number 4. That's the Official Note, one page only -- half a page, actually. And attachment number 5, another Official Note. So in this tab we have three documents: The record of on-site investigation and two official notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic if you go to the second page of your on-site investigation report - for the Court it's the third page - we can see that the document, whether dated or not, covers at least the 26th of May. So it goes beyond the 24th and 5th of May to the 26th of May. If you'd now, please, come back in the Serbian version to the first page, I think, and certainly in the English version, the English translation, to the second page. We see a paragraph that's headed or titled "On-site investigation - continued," and it says: "On the 24th of May, the same investigation team, joined by Slobodan Radovic ..." Do you find that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's on page 2 in the original as well. At the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That says: "Upon inspection of the premises --" "... of the scene -" I beg your pardon - "the atrocious consequences of the bombing that lasted for several days have become obvious. Dozens of killed inmates were found in the prison mess, presenting a horrid sight. There is a hole several metres in diameter in the ceiling or roof structure of the mess through which the sky can be seen. Forensic technicians collected fragments of aerial bombs ..." Now, will you please just confirm that this document that includes that passage contains absolutely no reference at all to any alleged bombing at 6.00 on the morning of the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passage that you have read certainly doesn't mention that. I don't know if there is another passage where it is mentioned, but you are right as far as this paragraph is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed in this report itself, that is not mentioned. If we go to the Official Note, which is the next document, as the accused reminded us and as His Honour Judge Bonomy I think has already found, we find the Official Note that we've looked at before, apparently dated the 22nd of May, 1999, coming from Bojic, which concludes with the paragraph: "According to subsequent information, NATO continued the bombing on that day from 1700 hours to 1805, and then again at 2310; another attack took place on the 22nd of May at 0610 hours." Now, let me make it quite clear to you: My suggestion is that documents that suggest in one way or another bombing at 6.10 in the morning or documents such as the one we were looking at earlier which ascribe all deaths to the consequences of the bombing over a period of days have been created in order to mislead and to hide the truth.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely cannot confirm or agree with your suggestion, Mr. Prosecutor. During the examination-in-chief, we saw that this reference does exist in some other document as well. We see it here in a document created by an investigative judge. There may be certain contradictions, but any contradiction contained in these documents would require additional verification. At this moment I can simply not state anything one way or another because I don't know. None of these documents are mine. Yesterday you used the term "fabrication." If any fabrication took place indeed, then everything would probably fit in. These contradictions tell me that there was no attempt at cover-up. Documents were created that contain certain contradictions. Why they are there would require additional checking. I cannot tell you at this moment why a certain reference exists in one document but not in another --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But why --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because none of these documents, as I said, are mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why did special units, of which you must have been aware, take the prison over at very short notice from 5.00 on the morning of the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a clear answer even on that. The prison administration falls within the local purview of the police station in Istok and the Secretariat of the Interior in Pec. That is where this incident involving loss of life happened. Nobody should issue any orders to the local competent police for them to go on site and take all the measures prescribed by the law. Why they went there at those particular hours I cannot speculate now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what's your position on the bombing -- the alleged bombing at 6.10 on the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry I hadn't made it clear. That's a complete --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's also part of your fabrication allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The allegation is that at 5.00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow the relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and from that moment on there was no bombing, and that any allegation of bombing from midnight on the 21st is a cover-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And my suggestion is that's actually supported by the material we have here. Can we look at one more document, please, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this document that you're looking at, which is dated the 4th of June, says: "In relation to an order of the Court --" it comes from Rakocevic again, who is referred to in the accused's documentation, "-- forwarded me from the MUP Pec, I inform you of the following: "It was not known to me on the 21st, 24th and 25th of May that an on-site investigation was conducted by the Investigating Judge because I was neither present nor was I informed about it." Don't you find that a little odd, Mr. Stevanovic, that the governor of the -- the chief warden of the prison was not even informed about an investigation happening at his gaol?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it does appear odd. That's precisely what I said in response to one of the previous questions. For the prison warden not to know where about a thousand prisoners are being evacuated. Look at the next paragraph, though. He says: "I do know that the investigations started on the 21st of May, 1999 ..." So already in the next paragraph he says he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... read it all then, please, if you want to. I'll read it to you a little more swiftly, and follow it in the original. "After the 21st of May ... all activities related to the newly arisen situation at PCI Istok were taken over by the authorised SUP organs and the Investigating Judge. I do not know how far they got with the on-site investigation. Therefore, I was not able to act according to the order since do I not have the requested information at my disposal. "Regarding the security employees, they were all present in accordance with the regular rota, and those wounded were --" and then he names and identifies them. Last paragraph: "Due to the resulting situation at the institution following the arrival of the MUP employees on the 22nd of May at 0500 hours --" and perhaps you'd be good enough to read from the original the last sentence that the translator found difficult to read. Can you read the last sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence is: "Due to the resulting situation at the institution following the arrival of the MUP employees on the 22nd of May at 500 hours, employees of the security service of the PCI Istok were not present." That is the wording of the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, then, Mr. Stevanovic, if you can't tell us what the people were doing deployed at 0500, can you tell me where I should go to find the written orders, the written records, et cetera, of what they did?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only place where one should look for such documents are the SUP of Pec or the municipal or district court in Pec, and of course the prison administration. I'm certainly surprised that the deputy prison warden is not aware of the facts related to the prison he is administrating. We should establish the reason why he doesn't know. That, of course, is only my assumption, and all that I have said, in fact, is only an assumption because I don't really know. I'm seeing the document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That surely was a misunderstanding of the question. I think the question that was put to you was where would Mr. Nice obtain the orders that related to the attendance of the MUP at 5.00 in the morning, not the investigating judge and the SUP acting with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that I misunderstood, but I answered that question too. The address where you could find such documents is the Secretariat of the Interior in Pec. That is the instance that is qualified, has control over that locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought yesterday you told us - I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - that for the deployment of SUP or MUP officials to take over a prison in the way that is clear this prison was taken over would require very high authority. Are there going to be ministerial records that will show what happened in respect of this prison at 5.00 on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that I have never said that any action of the police in such a case would require a decision from higher up along the chain of command of the MUP. It could be a case of misinterpretation. I said several times that in case of such incidents --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the local competent police acts according to the law without any special instructions. And of course this is not a case of take-over, although this word may be used some way here, but in my understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All the signs here are of the Ministry of the Interior, one part, at least, taking over a prison. I don't know if the prison falls under the Ministry of the Interior. It may do. But is it normal for the police to be able to enter and take over control of a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prison without any authority from a fairly senior position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it's not normal for the police to enter a prison and take it over. We agree on that point completely. But I never spoke of any take-over of the prison. I spoke of police action, regular police action, in cases of incidents involving loss of life. There is regular procedure for that, and no special instructions or orders are required. The police administration is aware of that, and they are required to call the police and the investigative organs to come and perform their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, I'm going to make my suggestion to you crystal clear and I'm going to ask you just to look at a couple of documents and we'll move to another topic. My suggestion to you is that you and indeed this accused, as you know and he knows, know full well that this was a cynical, planned massacre, and you are here determined to defend that position on behalf of this accused. Do I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true, and I must say that I am deeply offended by the suggestion, because I came here to testify to the facts that I do know, and you are practically accusing me in front of this Trial Chamber, and I would like the Trial Chamber to protect me if this is not supposed to happen. I have said that no such plan existed, and I have never been aware of anything remotely similar. I have explained in detail all that I know. You continue to examine me on things that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, you have asked for the protection of the Trial Chamber. Mr. Nice comes from a tradition of vigorous prosecution, and that is wholly consistent with the tradition in this Tribunal as well. You don't require any protection. You answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is one of many photographs --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is one of many photographs from the area where the prisoners were found, the photographs taken in August of 1999 by the Danish forensic team, and the evidence would suggest no bomb craters but marks of this kind on the ground. Exhibit 165, tab 9, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Prendergast, if you would be good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From such marks on the ground the experts were able to trace definable lines of fire, as shown here; football field, volleyball ground, basketball ground, all in the sports area, from different directions. Did you at any time in your perusal of the materials provided by the Serb authorities find record of gunfire shots on the ground? Did you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In none of the materials that I reviewed have I found reference to any traces of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nor indeed in the forensic examination of Dubrava carried out by the investigative judge did you find any adequate examination of the ground at all, did you? Because there was superficial examination of the bodies, burial, and end of story.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what was done, and I have certain information that the on-site investigation was interrupted at least two times and was resumed three times, and from what I saw I could conclude that the on-site investigation was not performed quite meticulously as it was supposed to and as would have been normal procedure. But I think that was due to the ongoing danger and risk.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no sense in wasting further time, because this witness cannot help us with forensic issues. And as you know full well, as Mr. Nice knows full well, and I know, too, those -- that forensic evidence, seeing that it dates back to the August, has no value whatsoever. Those traces could have been left by the KLA in the meantime. And if they wanted to fabricate that story, they could have done anything to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, you may consider the value of putting questions of that type to the witness. He has already said he doesn't have forensic expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would, in the ordinary course of events, ask some further questions, but in light of the pressures on time, this is a very important matter that I wanted to explore because of the nature of the allegation I'm making against both the accused and the witness, but I think if I simply draw to the Court's attention that there's a whole Spanish team's investigation and there's also the evidence of the ballistics found in the bodies, to which reference has already been made, and I'll move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that plan an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's its tab number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember. I saw this diagram before, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's in the materials that have been produced, as indeed has the Spanish team's analysis; 165, tab 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the ballistics evidence and so on. And Your Honour, as I have perhaps already indicated, it also seemed to me fair to put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 8 is the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the videotape, and there's also the written report as well, with conclusions. And Your Honours, it also seemed appropriate to put my allegations, or the Prosecution's case, to this witness in the fullest detail given that I am going to make an application in respect of additional evidence, reopening or rebuttal as it may be. I'll move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to deal now with some more general points, Mr. Stevanovic, before we return to particular sites that feature in the indictment. These are general points of -- on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at Exhibit 319, tab 32. This is a document, Mr. Stevanovic, found in the Pec police station. Date not entirely clear but January 1999 is the subject of the first substantive paragraph. In light of what you've said about the attitude of troops and police at the time, between 1998 and 1999, can you help us, please, with why under "Objective" it should be said in an ambush plan: "To prevent the movement of terrorists on the above-mentioned local road," and to "eliminate the said terrorists ..."?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this document is genuine - I do see a signature here, the signature of Borislav Vlahovic purportedly, although I'm not sure it's his signature - then the objective as defined here is formulated in a partially lawful way, with the proviso that it is not clear what "elimination" is supposed to mean here. If what is meant is to kill the terrorists, then it is not a legitimate aim at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Likewise paragraph III, "General tasks," under monitoring the said road, et cetera, et cetera, and then: "... Upon identification of the vehicles and their passengers, use concentrated fire to neutralise and eliminate them."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the accused have a copy. May I ask whether in the B/C/S the translation of the word is correctly "eliminate"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The term "liquidation" is used here. I have explained in response to one of the previous questions that that term has a broad and a narrow meaning. In the narrow meaning it means to kill with premeditation, and in the broader sense it means to neutralise terrorists as such; to disarm them, to pacify them, to make them disband, to make them disappear. But if it is used here in the meaning to kill, then I can confirm that this position as expressed here is not the official position of the Ministry of the Interior or the policy of the Ministry of the Interior in the combat against terrorists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this document that the general is seeing now for the first time - and the same goes for me - it is absolutely necessary in order for him to answer any further questions to have time to read it in full. In the preamble of the document, it is said that the terrorists located in the Jablanica village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll hear the accused. Yes. Just finish what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That this plan here relates to a precisely defined group of terrorists. It says they use Opel Ascona cars, a white Mercedes, a white Lada Niva with an installed Browning heavy machine-gun, et cetera, et cetera. So all of this refers to the liquidation of an identified group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have the point, and the witness no doubt has it too. If the witness wants to have the entire document read, then he's entitled to that. If he wants time to read the document in full so that he knows the entire context in which the particular question is being put, he's entitled to have it read. And you, Mr. Milosevic, know that this is a matter that you can raise in re-examination. So that if you feel, General, that you are disadvantaged at any time by having a particular section to you without the other sections being brought to your attention, then that's a matter that you can raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, would you go and look --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Of course it is always necessary when I am handed a document and when I see it for the first time to see who compiled the document and who brought it in, and now the question here is whether the document was put into practice, what it says in the document. Thirdly, in my many years of experience I have had any number of cases where my subordinate writes a document which is -- does not correspond to the law, and I had to send it back at least five times so that the text does conform with the law. So I would have to know more about this text and document, whether it was acted upon, and I'd have to look at the entire context. Here the term was used as it was. Of course it is very important to see whether the plan is directed against concrete identified terrorist groups so that there can be no consequences on any innocent persons. And the fact that it says that doesn't actually mean that somebody is going to wait in ambush for such a group and to kill it without any attempts to apprehend the persons and take them arrest, because the procedure is to use weaker means first of all and move on to stronger means, not to liquidate straight away. And I have already explained, of course, that the consequences of any action can result in death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you go to VIII, please. The Chamber's page 3, but you will want to look at the original as well to make sense of what I'm going to ask. The original, although it was subsequently crossed out, contained a suggestion that each squad should have hand-held launchers with 30 bullets manufactured in China. The only reason for having bullets manufactured in China would be to ascribe action falsely to the KLA. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find the passage you've just read out first. I don't seem to be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Top of page 4.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does say manufactured in China, but then you can see that that was crossed out. So I don't really know why manufactured in China is mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document generally, I suggest, shows what I was asserting yesterday and will continue to assert to you; that there was a determined plan to wipe out the KLA, and by unlawful means if necessary.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan to eliminate the KLA undoubtedly existed. So the plan to eliminate terrorism from Kosovo did indeed exist. It was a firm plan at all levels, and it was consistent right down the line. But there was no plan for terrorism to be wiped out using unlawful means. I claim and state that the overall policy always consistent from top to bottom, that terrorism should be eliminated, that citizens should be protected, and that law and order should be brought to Kosovo and Metohija, but not including unlawful means. And I could just add that despite the fact that I always claim, and I claim now too, that it was the position that terrorists cannot be liquidated as intent, as a premeditated intent, of course does not mean that it is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm going to have to cut you short on answers unless the Chamber thinks it's wrong for me to do so because of the limitations on time. When you've answered something, we'll move on. If we now look, please, at your diary for possibly a little later on but roughly the same period of time, the 15th of February -- I beg your pardon, 14th of February, which is part of tab 440 of your own exhibits. And in the English version it is page 39 and 40, I think. 39 will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Binder 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't seem to have it, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the -- sorry. It's actually page -- can we go to page 40 of the English, and it's R0172392 in the top right-hand corner for you, Mr. Stevanovic. Hand-numbered page 28. 28. Do you have that page?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 0172392. Is that the right page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the 16th of February, reflecting a meeting of a collegium of -- the collegium. You'll tell us what the collegium was. What was the collegium composed of? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the collegium of the minister was made up of the minister's assistants and the heads of the departments at the headquarters of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And what we see is this, under number 1, first bullet point: "Together with the Pristina Corps, the finishing touches are being put to the plan for a broad anti-terrorist operation in the period between the possible airstrikes and the entry of ground forces. "Sending all OPJP or PJP detachments." There was a clear expectation, was there not, that you would have an opportunity to eliminate the KLA between, in the short window of time between the bombing that you expected and the arrival of ground forces. That's what that means.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states clearly that there is an anti-terrorist plan for the period from the airstrikes to the entry of NATO ground forces, and that is a plan -- the plan that I spoke about. I can't identify it in concrete terms. I think there were two such plans, one in 1998 and one in 1999, and I think that is the plan that is referred to here, the 1999 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was the willingness to act illegally in that period of time that led to some of the gravest crimes with which this accused has been charged. That's my suggestion to you. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Not at any single point did anybody ever utter or did anybody even think of acting against the law, unlawfully, against terrorism.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please define for me whether something which is anti-terrorist operation, termed anti-terrorist operation for the police or any other state organ is contrary to the law, unlawful, for Mr. Nice to be able to carry on wasting time in this way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's a comment, really. That's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now turn in the English to -- yes. I mean, what was the -- how long did you expect the bombing to last, Mr. Stevanovic, all of you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say, to be quite frank. I expected -- I didn't expect there would be any bombing, despite all the assertions that there would be. My evaluation and estimations were wrong, if you want my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to inquire. Was the position that you expected the bombing period to be short but nevertheless a period where you could have your way with the Kosovo Albanians, blaming what was necessary on the bombing?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. That observation is simply not correct. If there were bombing at the time people thought that it was necessary to undertake more serious -- more serious measures against terrorism, because then it would be quite clear that the terrorists would take the side of the aggressor. So because of that, it was logical that by engaging additional forces more decisive action against terrorism should be taken. And everything that I spoke of earlier on was a tolerance of terrorism despite the fact that we were dealing with terrorism to avoid conflicts and so on. So we were tolerant. But if the bombing were to start, then the situation was clear: We had to enter into an uncompromised struggle against terrorism in Kosovo because it was quite obvious that the terrorists were ground -- NATO ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... people didn't know what to do and that all the problems that they were facing led to their moving out of the country. Is that your -- is that your account for the population movement still?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said exactly what it was. Yes, I did say that and I claim that now, and I went on to explain the situation that we were facing when the NATO bombing started, and nobody could even have assumed what that would be like. And what I said before that relates to the period before the bombing and weighing up the situation as to what would happen if the bombing actually went ahead, but nobody could have envisaged that it would be such horror, such terror, such panic and such general chaos. So it's one thing what we assessed and thought would happen and it's quite another what did actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's see what did actually happen. At page 94 in your diary, which you can find on page R0172437, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could have that on the overhead projector. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a meeting sometime, probably the 3rd of May or thereabouts but before the 4th of May. Have you found the entry?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 437, are they the last three digits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 437 shows the date the 24th. ERN number 437 being the last digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see the entry -- well, if the Court -- if the Court would come back one page, then, to page 93, and we see -- Do you see an entry that begins on page 74 in handwriting, with the printed number 2438? Do you have that page?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. This is a meeting. We'll look maybe in due course at item 3, which says, "Clearing up the terrain," but just go over to item 4 and then we are back where we were, Mr. Prendergast. "Results of the operations: "Last remaining large groups broken up. "About 2.000 liquidated - many more than previously in a single operation. "Left the country - 900.000. "Terrorists remaining - 1.000. "Civilians remaining - 300.000." Was that a satisfactory result for those of you who were supervising this campaign, to have got rid of 900.000 people?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very often have to say that your observations are not correct. I apologise, but I have to do that, because you very often have incorrect statements and observations. Now, here it is obvious that either through some fault or something else the wrong term was used, or perhaps a term was used to bring together several terms and facts that couldn't be brought under that heading. So 900.000, let me say first of all, is a figure that I've never seen. My information says 800.000. 900.000, I can't believe that that figure is written down there. So we're talking about the consequences of everything that happened, not the result. A result would imply that that was the goal. Now, to break up remaining terrorists groups, that could be a result because it was a component part of the plan, to break them up. The liquidation of terrorist groups, conditionally speaking, can also be considered to be a component part of the plan, but this idea of 900.000 people leaving the country, that is not a result and not the result of the plan, just as terrorists remaining is not a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's your handwriting, you see?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what does "residents" mean, this heading residents? Yes, that's true, it would appear that this is my handwriting throughout the diary. It is. That is incontestable. But with the reservations that I have made and the provisos I have made with respect to my diary, and you know what they were. I don't want to have to repeat it and go back into private session to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me what these statistics relate to. Do they relate to a single operation, over what area, and over what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, if you ask me -- if you're asking me, Your Honour -- are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you can help, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, taking into account my reservations, I don't see the date here, I don't see what meeting we're talking about, I can't see whether it was my opinion or whether it was just my note, my jotting down of some information given by someone else. So it is difficult for me to state my views, but as to point 4 itself, I've already stated that there are several theses and ideas that can't be placed under one heading, quite obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's plainly sometime around the beginning of May. The next entry is the 4th of May and there's an earlier one the 29th of April. You accept that it's your handwriting, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle I do accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying any part of it is not in your handwriting? Let's be clear about that first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I explained that earlier on. I can't find the passages. I'd need time to do that, but in the diary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. But in this passage is part of it not in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't state my views. It would appear to be all in my handwriting. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you wrote -- you wrote 900.000. You wrote about 2.000 liquidated; and you wrote civilians remaining, 300.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably that is correct. Unless some -- there was some abuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even to that question about your handwriting you can't give a simple yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot because of the fact, Your Honour, that I explained in closed session, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that you may be able to identify parts of your diary which -- for which you're not responsible, but what you say about this is "most probably." Now, what is it about these entries that makes you have any doubt whatsoever that they are yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll explain that, and that's the most important point. I have been led to doubt this figure of 900.000. I was never aware of that particular figure. 800.000, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you write the 9 or did you not write the 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I say, I most probably did because the handwriting resembles my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not actually questioning the authenticity of the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, you know, because you were there on a daily basis, that there was planned, supervised, forced expulsion of Kosovo Albanians against whom allegations of KLA involvement could never be made. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that, and that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know that the Serbs in Kosovo, under cover of the bombing, took the opportunity to kick out as many Kosovo Albanians as they did, and 900.000, or you recorded as 800.000 at another place in your notebook, was a pretty successful result and not one about which you were remotely unhappy.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both observations are incorrect. First of all, this consequence did make me unhappy. And the previous statement is incorrect. It is especially incorrect when you say that the Serbs expelled the Albanians. What does that mean, the Serbs? It would appear that the citizens expelled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let me give you some examples from the considerable quantity of evidence that we've had in this court from a witness whose 92 bis statement is Exhibit 108. You police told residents to leave within five minutes at Suva Reka, burning houses and shooting at people. Now, can you say that's false? Do you allow it to be true? What's your position as the senior representative of the police there on the territory?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have also explained that fact a number of times already. Official policies, official plan and positions, element of the plan to suppress terrorism was to protect the citizens independent of their ethnic -- ethnicity. All anti-terrorist action was directed exclusively against terrorists. All the other citizens were the object or, rather, the subject of protection on the part of the security forces in Kosovo overall. And of course people did die, both Albanians and Serbs and policemen and terrorists and soldiers and of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short and I'm going to suggest that some of your long answers are designed to consume time and if you'd be good enough, please respond to my questions. I'll name you another person and then I'll ask you another question. A witness called Osman Kuci, whose statement was exhibited as Exhibit 109, in Suva Reka spoke of your police - and I'm going to call them "your police" - telling witnesses to leave within five minutes or to be killed. Can you say anything? Can you say that that man's account is wrong?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I of course am not going to say that his account is wrong but quite possibly -- and quite possibly his account is truthful and exact. But then I say that that is a case that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must let him finish, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was outside control, was beyond control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And of course I'm not ashamed of my police. On the contrary, I am proud of my police. But not the police that perpetrated this. The policemen who perpetrated this perpetrated a crime, and anybody who committed a crime like that deserves to be punished and to be put in prison, so I would like to warn you of not going into generalisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. Stevanovic. Now, will you please, in this mass of material you've brought -- no. I'll preface this with one other question. You are aware, of course, not only that allegations about ethnic cleansing by your police have been made in this Court but they have been recorded Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. since 1999 -- been recorded in detail since 1999 in researched books like "Under Orders" of Human Rights Watch, or "As Seen, As Told" volume 1 by OSCE. You know about that, and I want you to tell us, please, now, where in these volumes of material that you've brought we can find one evidenced investigation by your police, by your justice department, of somebody charged with ethnic cleansing, with forcing somebody out of Kosovo. Where can we find it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't help you out there where we can find it, but I did give a number of examples in which the perpetrator of a crime was a policeman, the policeman was apprehended, and legal steps taken. And bear in mind that we left Kosovo and Metohija at the very end of the war and that it was impossible for us to carry on investigations there. So rest assured that had we been able to do so, a large number of policemen and soldiers and citizens would have been investigated, prosecuted probably, and even convicted if there was time for that too. But the fact that we were no longer there, that we are no longer there, that we left when the war ended did not give us the opportunity of continuing our investigations on the basis of the documents that I brought in here and on the basis of just as many thousand documents in the MUP. And those investigations can be continued today, too, on the basis of the documents compiled by my police, as you called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have a word to say about the prosecutions, such as they were, that have been brought by the MUP of Serbia in respect of this war later, but please now help me with this: Are you saying that there has been at any stage an investigation, a thoroughgoing investigation by the Serb authorities into ethnic cleansing in Kosovo? And, if so, can I see it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to ethnic cleansing, as you term it in general terms, of course the concept is clear, but I can't state my views. I don't think it was. But about all specific events where the elements of a crime were uncovered, an investigation was started, there were documents compiled, and they are in place for a continuation of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at page 86 of your book, which is R0172432. This is for the 24th of April. Bottom of the page, please, Mr. Prendergast. Reference to treatment of civilians who are returning, but then a reference to refugee columns. "Security. "Discretionary checks of persons, vehicles and cargo. "Going out over the border - not en masse. "Suspicious ones should be detained, processed, kept, arrested," and that's it. The rest should be let go, shouldn't they? It is your handwriting, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just give me a moment to see where it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under item 2.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Columns, refugees, then it says "Security." That's the first point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then it says --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Discretionary checks of persons, vehicles, and cargo." Probably belongings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's just make one thing clear, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nice read out the word "security," and in your transcript it said "security," whereas here in his official or, rather, working notes, it says "secure," "secure," which is different. To -- to -- [In English] to be secure. It can be translated that way. [Interpretation] In the sense of an assignment. He's writing down his assignment and to provide -- to make secure, when it says columns, refugee columns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I have your answer to my question about the entry on page --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise but I've either forgotten what the question was or I wasn't listening attentively enough because I was listening and reading at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The fourth bullet point, "Suspicious ones should be detained, processed, kept, and arrested." And I asked you what should happen to the rest? They should be let go, shouldn't they? That was what you--

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You wanted them out of your country. No reference here to counselling them to return, no reference here to saying advise them of security. No, just let them go.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. It does not say it here, Mr. Prosecutor, but I'm sure it does say so somewhere. And here I have just noted down several points which were topical at the time. So it's probably about a point in time when it was impossible to prevent anybody from going there, or leaving, as I have explained a number of times already. Not to incite them to leave, for civilians to leave. Of course. In the first point we can see that the objective is that the columns should be provided security, should be made secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can you help us with this, then: There's a great deal of evidence been given about organised, orchestrated passage out of Kosovo by trains and on buses supervised by the police. If you didn't want them to go, why were you arranging for them to leave?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, it is quite certain that the police did not organise their departure. The police did everything for them not to go, but they did not use force to make them go. I know very well that the organs of local self-government, transport companies, I mean even the police and army were under enormous pressure from citizens to have buses, trains, and other vehicles put at their disposal so they could leave and cross the border. Nobody organised this or used force to make people leave. With reference to transport, we can only speak of enormous pressure on everyone concerned to make available vehicles for them to leave in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, although I'll turn to this as a separate topic later, two questions about your alleged inability to investigate crimes committed in Kosovo. Can you point me to any investigations of Serbs forcibly displacing Kosovo Albanians in 1998?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall any specific events in connection with this, and I do not know to what Serbs you are referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe it's your position, and by all means state it if this is so, that there were no crimes committed by Serbs in 1998. Is that your position? If so, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my position that the Serbs did not commit any crimes in Kosovo. From the statistics I brought with me, one can see how many crimes were committed in what period and what action was taken in connection with these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second thing, just look at these documents. They're not exhibits. I don't particularly ask them to be exhibits either. The first document -- cast your eyes quickly when you get it, firstly over the 1999 document. Do you see the 1999 document? And I want to deal with this quickly. You see the 1999 document is a 30th of April, 1999 request to carry out an investigation of soldiers suspected of obtaining property from entering the houses of Serbs, indeed. Take a look at that. And if we look at the 2002 document, "In the name of the people," we find that in 2002 this is the same investigation against the same people being continued, right through to verdict and sentence.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you expect me to provide an answer of some sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, is that what the documents show? And then the question: Is that what the documents show? They show process begun in April 1999, concluded in 2002 in Nis?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this is the first time I've seen both these documents. One is a request that an investigation be conducted by the military prosecutor, and the other one is a judgement by the military court in Nis. These are military judiciary organs of the army of the then Yugoslavia, and they have nothing to do with the police of Serbia. However, I will answer your question, whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My general question is this, and we can look at other documents if I have time, which I doubt: In exile, or however you describe your position after June of 1999, but away from Kosovo, you had the potential to proceed with investigations and take them to conclusions if you wanted to. You the police, the justice department, and everyone else. Isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some proceedings could, of course, be taken to conclusions. Some were ongoing, and some could not be carried any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But nothing of any significance at all was started in respect of offences committed against Kosovo Albanians until after the fall of this accused from power in 2000, and even then only a very small amount; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that a large number of criminal reports were delivered to the competent prosecutors' offices while the police units were still in Kosovo. I know that proceedings were initiated at the time. These were continued. I really cannot say whether the speeding up or slowing down of a proceeding has anything to do with a change in government, but I do assert that all proceedings, whatever organ was in charge of them, were conducted pursuant to documents compiled by the police while they were still in Kosovo and Metohija. Of course, particular cases grew if they continued to be investigated, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to have to cut you short. But my question to you is this: The reason there was either no or almost no prosecution is because what was done on the territory of Kosovo by your police was done in pursuit of the objectives of your leader, the accused, and you couldn't possibly prosecute people when they'd been doing what you wanted them to do. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police in no way carried out any tasks in accordance with the wishes of any leader, as you say, but in compliance with the law. You must bear in mind that policemen in Kosovo were also victims. 400 policemen were killed carrying out these tasks and several thousand were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a very senior person are deeply implicated in all this, as is revealed by what you did to cover up the crimes. That's my suggestion to you, and to make it good we'll now look at the next exhibit, 283A, please. A man called Karleusa conducted an inquiry into the way the bodies of innocent victims moved from Kosovo to Serbia. He offered you an opportunity of talking to him. Did you decline?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct that I declined. I did talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make a full statement and give a full account of what you'd done in this matter, or not?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the things he asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll try and find it. I may not succeed today, but I'll try my best. This, on the other hand, is a statement made by Mr. Rade Markovic, Radomir or Rade Markovic. Just remind us, where is he now at the moment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Radomir Markovic is in detention, in custody in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For what crime?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stambolic -- you don't know?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know for what crime he is in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't know for what murder he's in detention. That's really your case, is it? Not your case, your answer. Something sensational --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know for what crime he's in custody. He has been linked to more than one crime, but I have not seen the indictment or, rather, the request for an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is the statement he made, and we'll place it on the overhead -- it is on the overhead projector and let's just remind ourselves of what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to remind you, both you and Mr. Kwon, who were here while Judge May was the Presiding Judge, this is a statement brought by Karleusa. Radomir Markovic testified after Karleusa, the person whose statement this is. It's all in the transcript. And he said very clearly that this was not his statement or, rather, that this is not what he said. Therefore, I fail to understand how Mr. Nice can use this document now in this way, because Radomir Markovic said here under oath that this was not his statement, and the statement was actually brought here by Karleusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The evidence, as the Court will recall, is that whatever the former police chief said about his ability to be persuaded to sign a document that was not an accurate reflection of what he had said, following the witnesses, namely the signatories, were also -- the co-signatories of the document were called to give an account of the circumstances in which the statement was made and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and it will be for the Court in due course to decide where the truth lies. I'm seeking from this witness a comment on the accuracy of what he's going to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I remember is that Mr. Markovic said this might be subject to liberal interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He didn't say it wasn't his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you follow with me from a few lines down, where he says: "... I know that in March 1999 --" it's about four lines down -- "a working meeting was held around a long table used for working meetings in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the library on the ground floor of the White Palace where Slobodan Milosevic most frequently held meetings. Stojiljkovic, Djordjevic, chief of the public security department, and I attended this meeting. This meeting was most likely devoted to the issue of Kosovo, and in addition to those listed was probably attended by representatives of the VJ, although I cannot say that for certain. Beyond the main topic of the meeting, at its very end, Djordjevic raised the problem of removing Albanian bodies to remove all possible civilian victims who could become the subject of an investigation by The Hague Tribunal. Milosevic ordered Stojiljkovic to undertake the measures necessary to remove the bodies of the Albanian civilians who had already been buried. I personally did not get involved in the conversation on this topic since none of the orders was directed at me. I know that Stojiljkovic appointed General Ilic to implement this task and that the latter then went with specific team of collaborators to the Kosovo-Metohija area. I personally did not want to allow the RDB to get involved in this morbid tale of later disinterment and removal the bodies so, as far as I know, it was the RJB and members of the VJ that participated in this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for a question now, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the next sentence, as you'll see, where the name becomes relevant, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Stojiljkovic issued the order to implement these measures directly to Ilic and Djordjevic. In addition to them, Obrad Stevanovic, Ilic, Djuric, Sreten Lukic, Dragisa Dinic, and probably all the members of the MUP collegium at the time also know of the order." Djordjevic was your superior at the time, yes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Djordjevic was the chief of the public security sector at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
