utterances.text: And just to deal with a small historical point, Djordjevic you will have seen on the Kula camp ceremony video. Do you remember he attended that in 1997? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I saw him on the video yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Djordjevic was a willing participant in this process of removal of bodies?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me say that everything that has been read out here as Rade Markovic's statement is untrue. There is absolutely no meeting which I attended and where such an idea was mentioned or anything similar to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily say you attended the meeting. It says, however, that you would have known of the order. Did you know of this accused's order to have the bodies removed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just remind us again: What's your explanation for the removal of bodies from Kosovo to North Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I have no knowledge about this whatsoever except for what I read in the media after the war, and at the time I did not believe it to be true. I can now say that I do believe it's true, but I have no explanation as to who could have done this and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive me if I misinterpreted you, but when you first gave that answer to the accused were you seeking to suggest that in some -- in some way NATO or other occupiers of the territory may have been involved in the movement of bodies? That seemed to be what you were suggesting.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this as an assumption in response to a question. If I say that there is no logical explanation for such an action when what happened is connected with the official policies and the official behaviour of the state and the police, then it can simply be seen as incredible. And what I said was just an assumption. I said that it was probably done by someone who did not want to conceal the crime but, rather, to prove there was a crime and to ascribe it to the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help me further, because this is very -- obviously very important. How could NATO, the UN, or any other country have access to Serb-controlled areas of military significance in North Serbia so as to deposit bodies there? It's something we'll want your help with.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say that it was done by NATO. I said it was done by someone who in my opinion might have had such a goal. That someone could be in Serbia, outside Serbia, in the police, outside the police, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's follow the workings of your mind and your imagination and your creative calculation. Who, and then how, but first who do you say may have moved these bodies to Serbia? Serbia's not been under foreign control, remind us. Who moved them to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say who specifically. I said someone who would have such a goal. Anything else would involve too much imagination, and you yourself said we should not speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a serious answer, Mr. Stevanovic, a serious answer that you're saying someone unknown may have taken all these bodies that come from Izbica and all sorts of other places, moved them to places that are in the secure control of the Serb authorities with vehicles, dig the holes, and put them in it? Are you really suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that was my assumption. I have no reasonable explanation for it. You had one assumption, I put forward another possible assumption. There are many other assumptions that might be put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The answer -- the truth is this, and I might as well put it now, I'm going to put it at some stage: Throughout your evidence you've been prepared to say anything to avoid a reliable and accurate implication against this accused falling on him, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you: You've been prepared to lie and to make things up in order to avoid the truth emerging from your lips.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look a little bit further, then, on this statement. Lukic, Dinic and probably all members of the -- knew of the order. In informal conversations held before the collegium, and at working meetings, there was frequent mention of so-called restoring of the terrain in Kosovo and Metohija. Next sentence: "I know that Dragan Ilic was not satisfied with the activities implemented by the MUP in this area, because of which he complained to me on several occasions of the difficulty of the job he was doing, his lack of preparation for such horrors, and the resistance he was meeting in the field from people who were supposed to assist in revealing the locations of bodies of Albanian civilians. In this context, Ilic told me that MUP Colonel Radosavljevic had offered him significant assistance in this job ..." Pausing there. First, Radosavljevic is the man we know about who led the attack at Racak; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he participated in that action, but I don't know whether he actually led the attack. Well, it wasn't an attack, certainly, it was just an operation. I assume that he did lead it. I seem to recall some information from some media, but I can't be sure about it. I am sure he participated and made some sort of statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Remember my earlier suggestion to you that you're taking time deliberately. Please keep answers short where they can be. Is what is said by the -- about the MUP here being involved --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. That is not my intention, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I agree, Mr. Nice. I think that's an unfounded -- there's no foundation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is what is said about the MUP's involvement here true, false, or may it be true?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must focus your question on a specific part of the text, otherwise I don't know what to reply, what my reply should be about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I've read that they weren't satisfied with the activities of the MUP but they got significant help from Radosavljevic. Is that true, false, or may it be true?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot concentrate enough. I cannot focus enough. I don't know what you're referring to. I assume you're referring to what was allegedly said by Dragan Ilic, that he had problems in Kosovo and that Goran Radosavljevic helped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look the another document if you find my questions about it not helpful. We'll move then, please, to --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can respond, of course, but I really wasn't focusing. I don't know what you mean. I offered you a response about what Dragan Ilic allegedly said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you wish to reformulate the question, then you should. Or if you wish to move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on because of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 100 of the diary in English, please, which is 0172446 for you. Have you found that page?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet, unfortunately. Yes, I have found it. 446 are the last three numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this is part of an entry. You can -- keeping your finger in that page, you might go back to find what you say is the relevant date for this page but it's sometime after the 21st of May, on or after the 21st of May. Is it your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few entries we might like to look at on this page. "Urgent end to burning and looting." Whose burning and looting was that you were writing about? Ten lines down. Sorry to interrupt you. Whose burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This point does not refer to anyone specifically but simply to putting a stop to the occurrence of burning and looting regardless of who was doing it. It cannot apply selectively to certain categories of perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it the MUP, was it the VJ, or was it some third body that we haven't heard about? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such things evidently occurred. The police can be ordered to prevent it through various forms of activity regardless of who the perpetrators were. The perpetrators could be civilians, policemen, soldiers, terrorists, whoever. However, this simply means that additional efforts should be made to put a stop to these occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then let's look at the next three lines on. It reads as follows: "Remove traces of violence against civilians," and then there's something that's not decipherable by us. What's meant by "Remove traces of violence against civilians?"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit odd here. It says here "Roads." It's probably traces of violence in connection with civilians. It has to do with clearing up streets and roads, making streets and roads passable. And the abbreviation should be civil protection, civilian protection staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, what sort of --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, please. This is why I'm concerned and have reservations. Had I put this away, it would really have been a problem. It says here "Remove traces of violence against property." It doesn't say against civilians. I'm trying to be brief in my replies and not to study the documents in too much detail, but here it says clearly, "Remove traces of violence against property." So this means rubble blocking roads and streets. You said civilians and I accepted what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please be good enough, and we'll just follow it in the -- in the original --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If there's a translation error, please just read the entry and we'll hear it translated.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says quite clearly: "Remove traces of violence against property."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll make that amendment if that's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So for "civilians" it should read "property."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may suggest one thing. The Serbian version should be placed on the overhead projector so that those who follow can see for themselves what is written because this is written in Cyrillic. The letter C in Cyrillic is similar to your letter Y, with a long dash at the bottom, and it is clear that what is written here is "property." What we should put on the ELMO is the Serbian version, not the English translation, which is incorrect. And I'm not suggesting that it is intentionally incorrect, but still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe this matter has been satisfactorily settled, Mr. Milosevic. We accept that the word should be "property" and not "civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on, shall we, to page 106 in the English which is R0172451. And if Ms. Dicklich can find that as well, and if Mr. Prendergast is able to assist us, can we have both 106, and if Ms. Dicklich can hand the -- point the relevant passage to Mr. Prendergast, we may be able to squeeze both onto the overhead projector at the same time. See if you can accommodate both at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the underlined word -- words going to be the subject of your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, not particularly. All of them are, but -- I see what Your Honour's point -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because in that case I would have it placed on the ELMO so we have the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That, I think, probably does the trick. Thank you very much, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This entry begins with a reference -- first of all, your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This, too, is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reference to "the president" at the top right-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- what does --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "president" is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who were you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure which president this is a reference to. It Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could be the president of Serbia, the President of the FRY, the president of the government, in other words the Prime Minister. It could be President Milosevic or President Milutinovic. I don't know if there is anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with both?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I attended meetings where both presidents were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If this is to do with the removal of bodies from the territory, if it is, which president would it be?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with which president was present, and whether there was any talk about the removal of bodies I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the content and see if that's going to trigger a recollection of what this meeting was. Does the first entry read - and we have both on the overhead projector - "No corpse, no crime"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's your handwriting. Read, please, the next line for us.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Back-breaking work on --" I can't make out the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could it be that -- that question?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On that issue."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Issue." Very well. Can you read us the next line, please.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They will use evidence on crimes to justify aggression."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next line.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next line is "Clearing up."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next line.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what it says is: "Simultaneous clearing up of territories."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next line.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Try. "When the mission arrives --" carry on.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make it out. That's the problem. I can see that the last word is "mission."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a phrase in there about --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When the mission arrives," approximately, but I don't know what the third word is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Clearing up the terrain the most important."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Stick on the line where you were about when the mission arrives. The word "difficult" or "more difficult" appears there, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say "more difficult." Maybe the first word is "more difficult."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We will find it more difficult to --" I don't know what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "We will find it more difficult to," is a possible interpretation. Well --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, what was the setting for this entry? You were sitting there with one of the presidents, were you? May we take that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I did or didn't, I really cannot determine from this. It really says "President," and it is probably a reference to a meeting at a president's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you tell me, please, what that phrase "No corpse, no crime" means.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have explained this during my interview in Belgrade. At that meeting, I don't know precisely which meeting that was but I do have a vague memory, one of the representatives of the security forces, whether it was the military or the civilian security, I don't know, warned against perfidious action by terrorists, namely that they are removing the corpses of their victims and the casualties of anti-terrorist actions only to gather them again later and place them in mass graves in order to blame these mass graves later on Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this really your account for this entry? They're speaking here -- the president is speaking here, is he, about the perfidious actions of terrorists?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's absolutely not the president speaking. The word "President" can mean that the meeting took place at his office, and that's probably what it means. I do have a vague recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. What, in his personal office, was it? Without him present, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I'm saying. If the meeting is at a president's office, he is of course present, together with all those attending the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... bush. As is said, the president here is this accused.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something I can accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can or cannot accept?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the next line. "Back-breaking work on that issue." If anyone was talking about the removal of bodies by the KLA in their own interests, why on earth write "Back-breaking work"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Back-breaking work" cannot be ascribed to anyone other than those working against you. The word used, "mucki."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The other meaning of this word is "perfidious," primary meaning is "perfidious."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That indicates that it is a reference to somebody who is jeopardising you in a perfidious way. You will notice that in all descriptions of terrorist actions the formulation "perfidious attack" is used. So this is a word most frequently used with reference to terrorists and their activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters said the other meaning of the word is "perfidious."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Perfidious," not "back-breaking."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I notice the witness's answers have been consistent with that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving to the next line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you want to say something, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to draw your attention, Mr. Robinson. I don't know English as well as your interpreters do, and I don't know the term back-breaking, but for me the word "mucki" in Serbian, which is a very heavy term, should be most of all translated as "perfidious." It is something underhand, perfidious, absolutely negative. It is not something you would use speaking of activities of your own side. You would use it to describe activities and dirty work of the other side, of your enemy. Everybody who knows Serbian would understand this. And from this -- this original, when we say "mucki rad," we cannot -- we shouldn't understand that as difficult work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At the end of this exercise, Mr. Milosevic, you may be a qualified interpreter, but what you have said is consistent with what the interpreters said, that "perfidious" is the translation. Are the interpreters saying that "perfidious" is the better translation or that it is the -- the primary translation, or what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My understanding from the interpreters was that it was the primary meaning. They didn't, as I understood it, exclude the alternative second meaning. I think they are reluctant, and understandably so, to turn themselves into expert witnesses in the booths. We'll clarify the matter a little further, working on the basis of "perfidious" for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see that they're acting as witnesses at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's explanation would be that in combination with the word "work," it is inconsistent to translate this term as "perfidious." You don't say "perfidious work," and people have been known to use terms loosely, so we interpret this as "back-breaking work." If it were combined with the word "attack," then it would be indeed "perfidious attack," and that is how it is used most often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the interpreters, and we'll turn to the third line, Mr. Stevanovic. "They will use evidence of crimes to justify aggression." Who is the "they"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reference to terrorists, and in keeping with my previous explanations, when the terrorists take away their victims and the dead, those who got killed in anti-terrorist actions, to later bury them in mass graves, they thereby create evidence of the alleged crimes of Serbian forces. In this context, I would like to remind you of the alleged mass grave in Pusto Selo and the alleged mass grave in Izbica. This part of the estimate about their perfidious activity I indeed found in the minutes of one of the sessions but I can't remember which.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the -- for me to understand your -- what you say is the interpretation of this note made in May of 1999, is that the KLA killed people, they take the bodies, having killed them, they find a mass grave, they bury the mass grave -- they bury the bodies in the mass grave. They then create evidence that it was actually the Serbs who killed these people, who will presumably be Serbs they killed, it may be Albanians, and in that way they then justify their continuing cycle of violence. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By using the media to show mass graves, combined with the explanation that these mass graves contain innocent victims of Serbian aggression or Serbian violence, they try to prove violent actions of the Serbian forces in Kosovo. That is an explanation of their perfidious activity with corpses. When we received those aerial photographs of Pusto Selo, I believe that was before Izbica, we all noted that such an estimate was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you mean "such an estimate was correct"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That this estimate, according to which they will use alleged evidence on our alleged crimes to justify the -- or explain the victims, the casualties of anti-terrorist operations. I can be more specific; that they would thereby justify our theory, our estimate. They in fact proved that it's true even before we found this mass grave in Pusto Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as Pusto Selo is concerned -- I'm so sorry. Since you mentioned Pusto Selo, let me just lay on the overhead projector, please, a page from Exhibit 106. It doesn't feature in the indictment, but since you raise it, this is what a well-documented and sourced account, further down, says of this event: "When the village was shelled on or around the 29th of March, many of the villagers fled --" forgive my discourtesy. I hadn't kept my eye on the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "When the village was shelled on or around the 29th of March, many of the villagers fled towards Danjane/Dejne, while others remained behind. One man who was in a wheelchair and took shelter just on the outskirts of the village, and another man who was hiding in the mountains gave an account of what happened. "VJ and paramilitaries surrounded the village and gathered the villagers into one place. They separated the women and children from the men. The women and children were ordered away towards the road on foot. There were more than 100 men left behind. After going through the belongings of the men, the VJ and paramilitaries, in groups of 10, started shooting into the group of men. Nine men survived the shooting and six others were burned alive when they were set on a tractor, had petrol poured over them, and were set on fire. A man who was in the woods said that he heard shooting coming from the direction of Pusto Selo --" "A man who was in the woods said that he heard shooting coming from the direction of Pusto Selo --" I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we received a note from the interpreters about the same word, "mucko," and I'm going to ask them to explain -- explain it. Apparently they have checked the dictionary. Would the interpreter explain the note which was sent, in the interest of transparency.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the note was handed in by a French interpreter, so the French booth can perhaps explain.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Okay. One interpreter in the French booth checked in the dictionary Serbian into French and found "mucko," which means "perfidious" and only perfidious or perfidiously, and "mucno," which means "with difficulty, arduously."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the word in the original B/C/S, "mucko" or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The original word in the document is "mucko," K-O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So does one take it, then, that the translation should be "perfidious"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure where I left Your Honours, but I've been reading out from the "As Seen, As Told" history of the hundred men being shot, the surviving nine, the six who were burned alive on the tractor, and then I come to: "The man who was in the woods said that he heard shooting coming from the direction of Pusto Selo around the same date and waited for three days before entering the village. Over 100 dead bodies were later found and buried by returning villagers. The villagers had been shot and some completely burned while others were partially burned."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stevanovic, this, as you can see from the footnotes on the document, even if you're not able to follow the English text, is a sourced account of what happened at Pusto Selo. Explain to me why you say that account is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain this to you, of course, because I don't know about an event like that nor did I have any information about an event that was described in this way. I said that the first information of an alleged Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mass grave in Pusto Selo we received from the aerial photograph which is here. I think we showed it on the overhead projector, in fact. So from that knowledge, from that information, the police acted together with the judicial organs, and you have three large binders about what the police did, what steps it took after it was informed about this alleged mass grave. And there you will find facts from the post-mortems for each individual corpse that was found in the grave, and all of them, all the bodies were buried afterwards in the corresponding graveyards in that region. And if I remember correctly, a certain number of people who were found in the graves were not from Pusto Selo. However, I'm -- I don't want to claim that but we can see it quite clearly here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that these are binders 13, 14, and 15 in the exhibits which were attached to this witness's testimony, and they're all documents that relate to Pusto Selo in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now go back to your diary and your entry on page 106 or the other page that you've already got open to you. This -- these entries, whatever the interpretation of the word "perfidious" may add to it, these entries fit completely, don't they, with the suggestion I put to you that there was a planned operation, and at this time, to move bodies away from Kosovo before land occupation of the territory would make it more difficult to hide the crimes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These entries have absolutely nothing to do with transporting the people killed from Kosovo in a northward direction to Serbia. These entries have only something to do with the way in which the terrorists acted, and that is where the word "mucki" was used. Now, if you look at the rest of the documents, you will be able to see, with the concept of terrorist activity, this adjective "mucki," "perfidious" or "treacherous" is used frequently to describe the way in which they acted from an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just look at the last -- the second to last line. "When the mission arrives, we will find it more difficult." More difficult to hide things, or impossible.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not possible and doesn't have anything to do with this, although I don't know which mission this refers to. I can't explain that sentence, actually, because if it is a mission, then it can be the Verification Mission and then the date doesn't correspond to that. And here we can see, and perhaps it's important for me to tell you that, I can't just find it just now, but had the date been the 21st, for example, 21st of May, then the 4th of April, then ten pages later you have the 20th of May again. So there are some pages here that have been not put in the order they exist in the original, so I'm not quite certain now what period of time the text was written; whether it was written during the war, before the war, I really can't say. Because this notion of "mission" isn't clear to me. I used it usually to denote Verification Mission. I don't know how else I could have used the word "mission," to denote what else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, date is a bit confusing. Page 97 it says 21st of May, and 103 it's 7th of May back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is no doubt about it, there is an incorrect ordering of the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't challenge that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going, if --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice says that he is not questioning the fact that the pages have been mixed up in their order, but he claims that what he has just quoted was something quoted from May 1999, although the mission, the word "mission" is used, and as the general has just said, that word and term was used to denote the Verification Mission, and judging by the sense of what it says, this must have -- must have been noted down before October 1998, before the arrival of the Verification Mission although there's no date here and he doesn't know where it is but he claims that it's May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Respectfully -- no, I won't say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we're going to hear a little later, you see, when we return to your evidence about places like Izbica, one of the facts for which there is evidence is that even where the Serb authorities exhumed corpses, those corpses found their way to Batajnica 1 and 2. Don't answer yet. I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to hear that there is evidence about places like Izbica where -- even where the Serb authorities exhumed bodies, some of those bodies found their way to North Serbia and to territory controlled by Serb forces. Are you suggesting that the movement of those bodies is in any way explained by the conception you put on this entry in your diary?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer the second part of your question first. That absolutely does not correspond in any way to any note from my diary. Now, let me answer the first part of your question. Precisely with that fact or by that fact that the corpses taken out of the ground were post -- examined as a post-mortem, photographs were taken, and I said that everything that happened was a great mystery in actual fact. This detail was particularly important in the conclusion that I presented to you earlier on and that I'm telling you now as well. So if in this binder here there is a document about some person who was -- who had been killed and who -- and whose body was found, exhumed, autopsied and buried, I don't know then what the reason would be for that same person killed to be found in some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the position quite simply this: That wherever possible, once this accused had given his instructions to move bodies from Kosovo that would reveal crimes, those bodies were moved in refrigerated trucks, one of which unfortunately landed up in the Danube? Isn't that the simple but overwhelming truth?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a simple truth and nor is it the truth. I've said on several occasions that I don't know of any case where the president of the Republic of Serbia issued any kind of order whatsoever to whoever, except possibly the minister when he went to see him, but I don't even know about that. Now, the minutes from the meetings that I attended I do believe are in existence and I do believe that they will bear out what I'm just telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The minutes from the meetings you attended. Well, which meeting was that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't, of course, remember any meeting as to time and period. I know that I attended, say, five or six meetings accompanied by the minister or accompanying the minister. At other meetings perhaps I wasn't present when I was in Kosovo. Some other minister might have attended. But at the meetings that I personally attended, we heard reports from representatives of the police and the army. They reported at the meetings. And then all the leaders down the chain of command, both in the police and the army, were present at the meeting. A plan was accepted that was presented, or reports that were read out, and that's where the meeting ended. And all the findings after the meetings and between two meetings came to the police from the respective leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if, as I'm going to suggest is the truth, the president you refer to in this note is sitting to your left in this very room, you're also aware that his chef de cabinet Goran Milinovic is being investigated or charged with destroying his archive of documents, aren't you? So they don't necessarily exist. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the fact that an investigation is being conducted against somebody for having destroyed an archive. I know that the chef de cabinet of the president of Serbia was brought up in the newspapers, but I don't know in respect of what. And this is the first time that I hear that the archive documents were destroyed from the meetings with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can you explain to me why, given that we have made requests for assistance to your governments over the years in terms that would encompass records of the type you've just referred, can you explain why they haven't been provided to us?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have nothing to do with those requests. From my general information, I know that the government of Serbia is investing every effort, significant effort in cooperating with the Tribunal in The Hague. However, that's just by way of general information. I don't have the impression that the government of Serbia and the competent authorities are questioning their cooperation with the Tribunal and that they are intentionally not complying with requests made. That, of course, is my impression. I'm not in the government myself and I don't have access to official information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have received information from my chef de cabinet, the state security service, or as it's called the security and intelligence agency as it's called now, confiscated my entire archives. So I'm going to ask you to issue an order for those archives to be returned to me, because I need them, and I assume they had enough time, sufficient time to copy the entire archive and that nothing can remain hidden therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Go ahead, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for the document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I remind you if you're serious about the request, that is governed by Rule 54 bis, as you well know, and if you put in an application which accords with those provisions, it will be considered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just add that that was my private archive that was confiscated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of the movement of the bodies from Kosovo to Serbia there were certainly minutes being -- there were minutes being retained, some of which we have been able to obtain - it may be all of them, I'm not sure - of the MUP staff based in Pristina. And if we look at this one -- page 1, please, on the overhead projector -- it says that the meeting was held by you and by Major Sreten Lukic. Was that a standard way of holding these meetings? The two of you held these meetings?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Time doesn't allow me to go into all of it, but may we just go to the entry by Branko Prljevic on our page 4. I suspect it will be your page 3. In any case, Branko Prljevic. Underneath his entry, he says there's a shortage of 30-millimetre ammunition and anti-aircraft guns, spare parts. I thought I'd understood you to say that the MUP didn't have such weapons. It appears they did.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did have weapons of this kind. If I didn't say it, then I probably omitted to say so just by chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Coo, who reminds me that the MUP staff minutes are in 68 to 73 of the tabs of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we move on to the bullet points under Milorad Jankovic's entry, and about -- I'll forget that one and we'll just move to the -- no, I won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for the slight delay. I'm working from two different translations. This translation I'm working from that's available for the Court only recently having come to hand, which explains the problem. But let's go right to the end of the English page 7, and the last page of the version that Mr. Stevanovic has.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the two of you are there, making your points, and it then says this: "The deputy Prime Minister of the federal government --" bottom of the page, please. Thank you very much. "Deputy Prime Minister of the federal government, Mr. Nikola Sainovic, joined in and said that it was necessary for the first stage of anti-terrorist operations to be completed today for the purpose of active defence and for the protection of territory and the border in case of a breakthrough by the aggressor deep into the territory of the FRY. He also said that persons who had been detained for perpetrating crimes should be held in custody until they are taken over by judicial organs." Other matters regarding the completion and execution of assigned tasks are then dealt with. Mr. Sainovic, as revealed by this document, had the power to give you instructions, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it cannot be considered that these are instructions. He attended the meeting, he gave his views, but of course as I've already said, that does not mean that he ordered anything. Because everything it says here, everything that is written, is authorisation of the police; that is to say keeping persons in custody, detaining persons, and that could last for a period of up to 30 days, according to the wartime provisions, and afterwards they had to be turned over to the judicial organs. I assume that was his opinion at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is that whatever the formal position about a Joint Command, the reality was throughout the period of the conflict with NATO, or whatever one describes it as, you were under instructions that came from Belgrade, through Sainovic by this time, and that you always did what you were told.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat, and I've been saying this a number of times: Orders were certainly not given through Nikola Sainovic or anybody -- or any other politician present. Each of the politicians present quite normally had an opportunity to analyse the situation and to present his or her views, but that does not mean that this was an order at all. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Politicians very frequently occupy a position that might not be in conformity with the regulations because they don't know -- they're not fully aware of them. Now, here we're dealing with obviously the presence of Mr. Sainovic at a meeting and his position and viewpoint with respect to certain issues. However, even if he were not there, had not been there, conduct with persons detained is regulated by the law. And every policeman knows about this. Even the lowest unit knows what conduct is expected of the police force vis-a-vis a detained person. There is no need for anybody to suggest it. But that was quite simply the position taken by that particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you point me, Mr. Stevanovic, please, to any documented example of you or your brothers in the army going against an instruction or an expression of view by Mr. Sainovic? Got lots of documents here. Think back. Point me to one.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately I didn't think along those lines, those categories and relationships. I can't really say whether we acted contrary to them in any instance but that doesn't mean we acted pursuant to orders from Mr. Sainovic. All that can mean is that we conducted ourselves pursuant to the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We must now take the break for 20 minutes. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at this one next, please, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document we just saw is -- resembles tab 70 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is tab 70, and I think the problem is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- but the translation is a bit different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We've been obtaining translations -- Your Honour, just give me a minute. Yes. We're now turning to tab 71, if there is a translation there, which I think there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 71, please, Mr. Stevanovic. This is a record of the minute of the staff MUP meeting held in 7th of May, 1999. Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic took part. Would you be good enough, please, simply to go to the last page -- sorry, not the last page, page 7 in the English. And that's in the -- I'll find it for you. The large -- the long opening address of Mr. Sainovic. And it's a passage that -- in the contribution of Mr. Sainovic it's two paragraphs before the end of his contribution, before Janicijevic speaks. Have you found it? I'm sorry not to have been able to flag it for you more swiftly.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the end of the passage relating to Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that case that's on -- go back one page, I think, and you'll find the paragraph that begins: "The president of the republic and the Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic, heard the report of the commander of the 3rd Army ..."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will read that out: "The president of the republic and the Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic, heard the report of the Commander of the 3rd Army and the MUP police staff of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija and the text of the statement was made public, representing a state directive and order issued by the Supreme Commander which should be relayed to all police commanders as a task assigned by the Supreme Command." Now, that's Sainovic speaking. Explain what it means if it doesn't show this accused's authority over the MUP. Do you want me to read it again? "President of the Republic and the Supreme Commander, Milosevic, heard the report of the commander of the 3rd Army and the MUP police staff of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija and the text of a statement was made public, representing a state directive and order issued by the Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic, which should be relayed to all police commanders as a task assigned by the Supreme Command." What does that show?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear that Mr. Sainovic here observes a clear-cut fact, an unchallenged fact; that the meeting existed, that Mr. Pavkovic and Mr. Lukic reported, and that from the meeting a text was published, a statement was published which in a way represents a state directive or order by the Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic. Therefore, nothing is said which wasn't well known at that point in time. And let me remind you that I showed in one of the tabs a document of Mr. Lukic and the text of the statement was sent down to all the subordinates to become apprised of and to use. That does not in any way mean that they, on the basis of such a text, should do anything that would be unlawful. And the text certainly doesn't contain anything unlawful or against the law. It is just information about state policy in a difficult time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I notice that the order, it says the order was issued by the Supreme Commander, but at the bottom it says that this was to be relayed to all police commanders as a task assigned by the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And His Honour's observation indeed generates my next question: What is the Supreme Command to which this document refers?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already explained this, although I wasn't, quite obviously, sufficiently clear in my explanations. When I hear the term "Supreme Command," it is the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY, and the staff of the Supreme Command is made up by the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia at a given point. So that is my conception of it and understanding. I haven't had occasion to read the text of the constitution or the law, the actual wording, but that is how I understand the Supreme Command. As far as I remember, there were some terminological problems with respect to that concept and notion but at this point in time I can't remember the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mean there were terminological problems at the time? You mean people didn't know how to describe their authority body? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. I'm saying that terminologically speaking there was a problem that cropped up. I can't remember the details of it. But just terminologically speaking. And I explained what I personally understand under that term and concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, I need your assistance on this a little more. You say, and I don't accept your answer, but you say that the Supreme Command equals Supreme Defence Council. Let me just tell you a little bit of history and ask you a question. After considerable efforts, we have obtained the authorities the Supreme Defence Council records up and until the beginning of the bombing. We have been told that there were no Supreme Defence Council minutes or records for the period after the 23rd of March. We have also been told that there are no existing records for the Supreme Command after the 23rd of March. Now, that's the history on the litigation efforts to obtain the records. In light of that, are you saying that there were Supreme Defence Council meetings even if we've been refused the minutes of them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot answer that question, and apart from that I'd like to say that I really didn't -- I'm really not a legal expert. And I've already said that in the near past I did not read the constitution or the law for me to be very specific. But I said what I understand and imply by that. That, of course, does not mean that I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understand your answer. Are you saying that at the time when you dutifully sat through this meeting, if you did - of course you did - and you heard Mr. Sainovic speak of the Supreme Command, are you saying that you sat there in ignorance of what he was talking about or are you saying that you thought to yourself, "Aha, the Supreme Defence Council." Which is it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clearly understood what it says here, what is written here. I understood it to be the Supreme Command. Now, my previous answer referred to what I consider to be the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it matter if the order's given by the Supreme Command or the president and it's simply relayed by some other organ?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Arguably not, Your Honour, but what -- to explain the position, by our request for assistance we've been attempting to identify the body through which the Supreme Commander operated, lawfully or not, and it's for that that I seek this witness's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, your answers - let me explain - constitute the following, correct me if I'm wrong: That you, the most senior police official, didn't know the nature of the body from whom you were taking instructions. Is that really your position?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I have been repeating this several times: We did not receive orders from the Supreme Command. Therefore, the police received orders down its chain of command. And this text of the statement was used so that the subordinate in the police force could be informed about state policy at that given moment and the positions taken by the Supreme Command. So I myself am not a member of the Supreme Command or a member of the Supreme Defence Council either. I know which regulations are applied in war and relate to police structure, and in this statement I'm quite sure there is nothing that is unlawful, but there is no duty on the part of anybody to apply any statement in which there is anything unlawful. Perhaps I'm -- I don't understand the sense and gist of your questions and therefore I'm unable to give you a specific answer, precise answer. Of course, I'm not the man best placed to deal with theoretical questions about what the notion of Supreme Command actually means, nor did I delve in that. I understood the document to be a statement from the Supreme Command meeting which represented a political position and stand with respect to the conduct of all state institutions at that particular moment, and quite obviously, it was a moment of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Throughout your evidence you have struck me as a very well-informed senior official. While I understand the significance of the answer you've just given in relation to fairly inferior officials in the police, I find it difficult to understand that someone in your position wouldn't have to hand the information about what constituted the Supreme Command. Now, can I take it, therefore, that what you call the Supreme Command is in fact the Supreme Defence Council and that you did not regard or you did not consider that there was any other body forming the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is what my answer means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So just last question on that, then. So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to draw your attention for you to be able better to understand this, because there are no mysteries here at all, that this is to be found in tab 65, that is to say the document, the act or decree of General Lukic which speaks about sending out statements by the Supreme Command. It says, "In a statement by the Supreme Command" at the end of the document. And you also have the statement by the Supreme Command there where you can see that at the meeting that I received General Pavkovic and General Lukic and that another member of the Supreme Defence Council was there of a total of three members. The third was the president of Montenegro. He wasn't present. So we had the other member present of the Supreme Defence Council and the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command was also present. And then it goes on to say what we were discussing here. Then it was published publicly. It was made public in the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: These are points you can make in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be that -- it may be that if Mr. Milosevic is in due course able to assist us on the structure of the Supreme Command he will do so through an appropriate witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as I move on to the next topic just, then, this,

utterances.speaker: MR. STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Must we interpret -- must we apply your interpretation of the structure to this document in this way: That Mr. Sainovic, an extremely senior politician with experience of the Supreme Defence Council, describes it in a minuted meeting using the wrong term? Is that what we must understand?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never understood that Mr. Sainovic was a member of the Supreme Defence Council. I believe that's what you said. I may be wrong. As for the second part of your question, I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case I'm going to move on. It's Exhibit 387, tab 46, then, we need to look at. This is an existing exhibit in this case, and it's dated 25th of May of 1999, and it comes from the army, 3rd Army Forward Command Post, and it's addressed to the MUP of Serbia. And in paragraph 3 it says -- bit further down, Mr. Prendergast, please. It says this: "The security regime in the territory has not taken root in the spirit of the law and on the basis of the proclaimed state of war. The best example is the operation of the joint checkpoints manned by the MUP and military police units, where there are frequent altercations because MUP members condone or openly permit evident criminal activities and plunder committed by their fellow MUP members as well as civilians, resulting in the misappropriation of a vast number of motor vehicles, technical goods and other resources from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Over the page, please. "It has been established beyond doubt, and we have already reported on it in regular combat and other reports, that due to non-compliance with the resubordination orders, some MUP members and to a considerable extent entire smaller units which operate independently on the ground are committing serious crimes against Siptar civilian population in settlements or refugee shelters - murder, rape, plunder, robbery, aggravated theft, and they then purposefully attribute or plan to attribute those crimes to units and individuals in the VJ." Now, what do you say to that comment by General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me say that it is highly unusual that I am seeing this document for the first time. It would have been logical if all these claims were made at the time this document was compiled, that the head of the staff should know about it; and had this arrived in the staff, I would certainly have known about it too. We can see that this appears to be an original document, but these are serious allegations by the army against the police which I was not aware of until now. I spoke of problems pertaining to resubordination, and this is the title of the text here, but I did not have any information to this effect or any information that was as serious as this. I can only say that this may be true or may not be true. This is the first time I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's break down what General Pavkovic wrote into two parts. Forget who the culprit is. What he writes makes it clear that there are serious crimes being committed against the Albanian civilian population. Can you think of any reason why General Pavkovic at this time would fabricate, make up allegations about the commission of crimes against Albanians? Forget who the culprit is. Can you think of any reason why he should make up the commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite honestly, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it reasonable --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that he was a very dependable man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it reasonable thus to infer, and I'm asking you to help us with this, that there were indeed serious crimes committed against the Albanian population in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that there were, yes, but all the crimes that we were aware of were dealt with, processed in the appropriate way. If anyone in the army had any knowledge of a specific crime, then it was indisputably the duty of that soldier or leader to either arrest the perpetrators right away or to submit a report to the MUP for them to act pursuant to their authority. Let me remind you that the police arrested a group of soldiers who were caught red handed committing a murder. You have the report here. It would have been logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to that in due course. Let's look at the end of this document. This is, after all, May of 1999. General Pavkovic, intelligent, educated, experienced soldier, was he? Was he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at "Measures Proposed: "In light of the above-said, and particularly the consequences already in evidence, which could, however, become much more important, the Supreme Command should take urgent measures falling within its jurisdiction to resubordinate the units and organs of the MUP of Serbia in the spirit of the constitution and existing laws and in accordance with the proclaimed state of war or annul the order on their resubordination and leave the command and commanding of the forces of the MUP of Serbia in the hands of the Ministry of the Interior - staff of the MUP and the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo-Metohija through the Joint Command as has so far been the case." Now, in light of the most recent questioning of you, should we be able to make sense of this paragraph if we substitute "Supreme Defence Council" for the phrase "Supreme Command"? Should we? The Supreme Defence Council should take urgent measures? Or, at the end ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that's what it should mean. But the document on resubordination was also signed by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. Rather, the chief of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia at the time. As I don't have the entire context of this document, I can conclude that the previously provided explanations and facts cannot be brought into connection with the act of resubordination or subordination, because subordination can only refer to combat activities, whereas what we previously discussed were crimes and criminality. The police are duty-bound to deal with crime, and no one can be resubordinated in this respect. So these are two different things that have been erroneously joined together. I have already said that there were problems in connection with subordination, but here these problems are being linked with matters falling purely within the competence of the police, and this was not the subject of the order on resubordination, based on what I read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your answer is, as I understand it, that yes we can make sense of this paragraph if we use the words "Supreme Defence Council." Can you be good enough, please, to read in the -- just read without comment the last sentence of this last paragraph. In fact it's all pretty well one sentence, I think, but perhaps you could pick it up from three lines up from the bottom on the left-hand side, where it starts to make sense. Just read it out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I start with the part where it says " ... and in accordance with the state of war that has been declared, either to annul the order on their resubordination and leave the command and commanding of the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in the hands of the Ministry of the Interior - staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija through the Joint Command as has so far been the case." Of course I have not previously observed that it says here "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't make any sense, does it? The MUP of Serbia wasn't instructed through the Supreme -- can I finish the question? It doesn't make sense --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't make sense to insert the words "Supreme Defence Council" there because the MUP of Serbia wasn't instructed through the Supreme Defence Council, was it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, from what one can see here, there is a contradiction because in the beginning of the sentence the standpoint is expressed that it is the Supreme Command that should take measures, and then at the very end an alternative is offered and that is that command of the police forces should be taken over by the staff of the MUP through the Joint Command. If it's the Supreme Command that is in charge, then mention of the Joint Command is superfluous. This is evidently the standpoint of Mr. Pavkovic about the role of the Joint Command. I still abide by what I said previously in connection with this body. I continue to assert that the MUP in Kosovo was not commanded by the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understand, Mr. Stevanovic, how it is that -- or can you explain, then, how it is that all the documents we look at suggest the existence of some other body, the Joint Command? Can you understand that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you have shown the documents you have, and of course I did not have most of these. But in these tabs, there are dozens of documents indicating that the police forces in Kosovo and Metohija were commanded by the top of the ministry through the minister, the staff of the ministry in Pristina, and the Secretariat of Internal Affairs in Kosovo and Metohija. If we look at this document in isolation, assuming that the others do not exist, then of course my answer to your question would have to be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The context here would suggest that Joint Command is something different from Supreme Command, and it -- in its context it seems to be referring to the command of the MUP as distinct from the command of the army or the army with the MUP resubordinated to it. So was there something, Mr. Stevanovic, something in the MUP hierarchy that could be described as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only if this concept can be used as a synonym for the MUP staff in Pristina. But the staff of the MUP is mentioned here alongside the term "Joint Command." So in this case the answer would have to be no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then I suppose just this last question: Have I understood it correctly from you that if one is to trace the paper trail of orders -- decisions and orders, directing either the MUP or the army in Kosovo during the conflict, one's looking at the chain that goes back to the minister concerned. Is that your position? If we're looking for the paper trail of orders, we have to look at something coming down from the ministry?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ministry of the Interior, of course, to the minister of the interior in the army to the chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the Court will understand that in our search for clarity on this issue we've also sent out RFAs that would cover such lines of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at tab 67. Quite briefly, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, I was the president of the republic and the Supreme Commander. So if it's of any assistance, I can tell you what the Supreme Command is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you can give evidence later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to assist you with an explanation. It's in the constitution and in the law on defence, so it's easy to read about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, a quick look at tab 67, document of the 13th of May of 1999. This one's going the other way round, as it were. It's from the Ministry of the Interior, signed by Lieutenant General Sreten Lukic, and it goes to the chief, and then it says at the end of the first paragraph: "At the mixed checkpoints and during patrols, tasks are performed jointly by members of the MUP and the VJ and the VJ members stop and check VJ members and vehicles while MUP members stop and check MUP members and citizens and their vehicles. "During work so far in general and in the work of the aforementioned checkpoints and patrols, the following weaknesses and shortcomings have been observed: "Inefficient, inconsistent and unprofessional conduct; "Arrogant, improper and impolite conduct ..." And so on. It goes on to say this creates a negative image of the police. So we have on the one hand the army saying there are really serious crimes being committed and the MUP are responsible, and we now have the MUP saying to themselves there have been some shortcomings in behaviour. Is the truth that there were serious crimes and that this document's a half-hearted attempt to reflect some acknowledgement of it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said more than once that there were crimes. We discussed some of those looking at the documents in these tabs. However, this statement indicates that there was awareness of errors and failures, weaknesses, and these are clearly identified in a public document. Attention is drawn to what was observed and request is made to remove these weaknesses. When we look at this order, which is, in a sense, criticism of subordinates, this is stressed so that subordinates will take it seriously, that is the fact that things were being done not fully in compliance with the laws and regulations. Attention is drawn to the improper manner in which uniforms are worn, caps, and so on. This is done to draw attention to the problem so that subordinates will deal with this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suggest to you there were serious crimes being committed against Albanians throughout. You know it, but there was some need to put something into documentation to cover your backs. This is an example of it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not dispute specific events and I explained them. But it was not the policy or the plan or the order or the standpoint. The policy was to suppress anything illegal, first of all terrorism and then any other illegal actions, regardless of who was perpetrating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I turn to another topic, one last question on terminological inexactitude. That's my today's test for the interpreters. If we can turn to the English page 119 of the diary. It's R0172461. Top of the page, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you found the page, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll put it on the overhead projector. If Mr. Prendergast would help, then we don't have a language problem. Mr. Prendergast, the Serbian is coming your way as well, just to make sure. It's really just the title of this I want, so you can lay one under the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've got one that says in the English, "Session of the Joint Command," and then it says -- it may be further up, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in Serbian too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We better have from you an explanation of what this -- is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What does it mean "Session of the Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from everything I said about the Joint Command, it's probably clear what this means. The only problem is in the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What does it mean, then?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that I most probably -- no, not most probably, certainly attended a session that was attended by people who, as I explained previously, made up the Joint Command, or some of those people. And I remember very well from the interview in Belgrade that this is the only place in my entire diary where this term is found. And I express my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. doubts as to why this is here with that date. It would be logical to have this down in 1998. It doesn't seem logical to have it entered in 1999. Maybe somebody mentioned that that was the name of the meeting and then I wrote it down as such. That would be logical. But I understood that we have minutes of these sessions, so it might be a good idea to check whether there actually was a session on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you see, we've had -- this is dated very clearly the 2nd of June. We've had evidence from a witness about attending a meeting led by Sainovic the day before. There was a Joint Command, wasn't there? That's what you wrote down. For some reason you don't wish to acknowledge it now.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I admit, and it's obvious, that this has been entered in my diary. I expressed quite a few doubts about it during my interview in Belgrade. You can check that in the transcript. I don't know why and how I wrote this down, because everything else I know corresponds with what I said during this testimony apart from this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you see, we've had this express denial from your government that this Joint Command existed in 1999, and now we've got your writing effectively that it does. Is there some kind of joint agreement to try to hide the Joint Command and the Supreme Command from this Court? Is there some endeavour to do that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. And since you mentioned the government, I can tell you with full responsibility that I am not in contact with anyone from either the previous or the present government. What I am saying I am saying relying only on my recollection of that period. By no means on the basis of an agreement with anyone, especially not someone from a previous or the current government of the Republic of Serbia. This is simply a fact. It says -- I've explained this extensively. I've expressed my doubts, and everything else I know does not confirm that the Joint Command existed at the time mentioned here. If you go through the entire diary, you will see that I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
