utterances.text: I'm going to move to something else. You have been asked about and have given evidence favourable to the Defence about Padaliste, Suva Reka, Izbica, and indeed Racak. Let's just put on the overhead projector, please -- can we place on the overhead projector, please, this photograph. I'll just tell you this is the photograph of a woman from Padaliste who gave open testimony that men in police uniform, or in uniform with police insignia, surrounded her house in Padaliste on the 26th of March of 1999, killed six of her nine children, of whom the oldest was 19 and the youngest was 2, her husband, and her mother-in-law. She explained that the probable motive for the murder was revealed by the fact that a policeman had told her that the family would die because her husband was a teacher for children at an Albanian school. Do you know anything to suggest that this woman has told us untruths?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know absolutely nothing. But when you put this kind of question to me and show me this picture, I have to express my deep regret for the suffering of this woman. I have no knowledge of this event, and I think that's what I've been saying all along. All I can say is that the police did not register this event. No such event was reported to the police and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I want to ask you next.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How could it be, Mr. Stevanovic, that a killing of this monstrous kind on the 26th of March by people in police uniform could go undetected, uninvestigated, and indeed untried? How could that be?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained all the problems that we were facing at the time. Let me be brief now. It's possible that something happened of the kind that we saw yesterday, that video footage, but I'm saying again it has nothing to do with the official conduct and official policy of the police in Kosovo. If the police had even a scrap of knowledge about this, be sure that you would have a case file and an investigation. Maybe we would not have a complete result, but action would have been taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Remind us, Mr. Stevanovic --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you cannot doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- what was it you said about Padaliste that was favourable to this accused. How were you able to help this Court in respect of Padaliste? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not intending to help the Court. I just mentioned something that seemed illogical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Padaliste --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was that that was illogical?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain way it was illogical, although of course in my opinion it doesn't matter that much. What seemed illogical was that several people with the same last name were casualties in a place where there are dozens of different last names, and the allegation was that soldiers and policemen fired at random across the village. If the fire was indeed random, then it's unlikely that people with the same last name would be killed in a village with almost a hundred people with ten different last names. But I didn't doubt at any point that those people were indeed victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On reflection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me draw your attention to the fact that the allegation of Mr. Nice is contained in paragraph 66; that the forces surrounded the village, fired at villagers who were running away, fleeing, and that's how people got killed. And the witness explained on that occasion that it was -- that it seemed illogical, and he's saying the same thing now. If you want to read it, you can read about it. It's paragraph 66(f).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On reflection, Mr. Stevanovic, do you take the view that you have nothing to contribute to the evidence about Padaliste?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, I don't think so. Which doesn't mean that evidence does not exist, but I'm sure it doesn't exist at the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, I have to note the name of this witness is not Limaj but Imeraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I thought I pronounced it correctly but maybe I didn't. It was on the transcript incorrectly -- sorry, it's on the film it's incorrect. Your Honour is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we look, please, at Suva Reka. We'll -- if you wish to, we'll find that in the indictment as well. Remind us how you feel you can help this Court in respect of Suva Reka, Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I answered questions on that subject too. In these case files, we can find two incidents involving nearly 20 people who were killed. There are also documents that the police and the competent judicial authorities drew up in connection with these incidents. If my memory serves me right, I said in response to a question that there could be no reason why the police would not act in the same way with regard to the incidents alleged in the indictment if it had had any information about them. So my response was that the police had no reports or information about the incidents cited in the indictment concerning Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The S-A-J, or SAJ as it's pronounced, is a body with which you are familiar, and it falls within your part of the MUP, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SAJ, S-A-J, the special anti-terrorist unit of the MUP, it belonged to the sector of public security, that much is true, but it was not within my purview, in my job of assistant minister. Nor was it in my purview at any other time before that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, although not within your purview, can you confirm that there was a firing range of the SAJ near Prizren?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, and I don't think that's right. I do know that there is some sort of firing range near Prizren, but I have no information that the special anti-terrorist unit of the police used it for their exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you can tell us is this: Firing ranges aren't open to the public, are they?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, no. I believe that one was within the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have a photograph of the witness, but I'll tell you what it was she said. We had a witness here called Shyrete Berisha, coming onto the overhead projector now - thank you very much - and she explained how on the 26th of March of 1999, men wearing green camouflage uniforms killed her four children and her husband. Altogether, 40 people were killed in the coffee shop by perpetrators who shot and threw hand grenades. She was wounded but survived, jumping from the back of the truck that had transported her, as if dead, and other bodies away. Now, the evidence, Mr. Stevanovic, is that those bodies were first buried at the SAJ firing range near Prizren, somewhere which, as you say, in principle, should not be open to the public. They were then exhumed by workers of the Hygijena company and loaded onto a refrigerator truck, and taken at that time nobody knew where. But in 2001, they were found at Batajnica at the SAJ premises there, the 13th of May training facility, facility under the public MUP's control. Can you explain to us, please, what was wrong with the system of policing of your territory that people murdered in this way could pass into one firing range that may have been or, as you would say, may not SAJ and land up in the controlled environment and premises of another SAJ training facility near Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me reiterate the statement that this training ground in Prizren was certainly not used by SAJ, because I cannot remember a single moment when SAJ were in Prizren. I know they were in some other areas. That's one thing. Second thing: All that you have described just now I already qualified in my previous answers. So I really do not know what could be the reason and who could be the perpetrator of this. This would have to be explained by somebody who was involved, who participated in this, because I have no knowledge of this, nor did I have any knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you were a very senior policeman, and if I may invite you -- and we're dealing with the real world here. For bodies to move from one controlled environment to another belonging to a police force is something that the senior officers and representatives of that police force should be able to explain, and I want you to tell this Court why it was this woman's family was moved about after they'd been killed in that way.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot help you with an explanation. All I know in this connection I have already said. I can only repeat myself. And in policework, I have already told you, when you are working on something that hasn't been elucidated yet, you always start out with several possible versions, and at this moment I cannot single out any of the possibilities, but I hope that this will be ultimately elucidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. I'm happy to go on as long as the Court wants but I simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we have stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I mention this: I shan't -- I had hoped, of course, to finish today. I shan't be long on Monday. But there was the possibility of this witness giving assistance in relation to certain matters and indeed I think His Honour Judge Bonomy raised it, as did I. We will provide him, if he would find this helpful, with the photographs and the names of the people identified or suggested as identifications by me yesterday, and if there were any other matters that he might usefully inquire into there is a three-day period for him to do so, but it's the photographs, with your leave, that I would make available to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Those photographs may be provided to the witness. You will recall, General, that you had indicated that you could make certain contacts. Of course, these contacts do not allow you to discuss the evidence at large, it's for a very narrow purpose, and you're not to discuss the evidence with anybody during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are now several more names in the Prosecution's exhibit, Mr. Nice, for the witness to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The only names that -- in the exhibit there are many other people, but I think the names are the only names that I'm presently in a position to put, and I put them, of course, both with names and with photographs so far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It wasn't only the photographs. It was also the documents that were produced in cross-examination yesterday, and the witness said that he would make inquiries, and it arose as a result of a question from the Bench, as to those members of the MUP named in the documents, which I should imagine the Court would have no objection for him undertaking those inquiries in the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he should be given the information to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that the documents have already been passed on to the witness. We are adjourned until Monday, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
